chapters.title: Chapter 8: A Plan Is a Line
Chapter 11: The Canyon Has a Beat

spans.text: The orange portal closed behind the crew with a warm pop, and the first thing Patch Bolt did was read the dust.

He could not help it. In Green Hills Lab, dust puffed and fell and got out of your way. Here it had weight. A grain lifted by a boot hung a beat longer than dust had any right to hang, then slid sideways and settled in a thin pale stripe along the next ledge down. The stripe was not random. It ran along a slow current of warm air, and the canyon, with its dust, was telling him exactly where its air wanted to go. Most builders walked through that and saw nothing. Patch saw a map being drawn for free, and he loved it for about twelve seconds.
Then a crate shot past him so fast it stole the dust from under his boots.

It went by at the height of his knee and the speed of a thrown wrench, and it made a sound on the way that Patch would have trouble describing later. Somewhere between a wooden bell and a complaint. It clipped a rail bumper, bounced, grazed a small rolling thing he barely registered, and vanished behind a sandstone arch as if it had business there and was already late for it.
A second later, something enormous rumbled under the canyon floor.

The rumble was not loud. It was deep. It came up through Patch's boots and registered in his knees before it reached his ears, the kind of deep that a body believed before a mind agreed to it. Up at the top of the cliff, at the far edge of his sight, a single rounded shadow shifted a quarter inch in a long curving channel, then settled back, the way a sleeping cat shifts and settles when a stranger walks into the room.
Proper problems,
spans.speaker: Ember

spans.text: Ember Slice said, spinning to watch the crate go,
usually introduce themselves first.
spans.speaker: Ember

spans.text: Patch's hand was already at his belt. His thumb found the orange tape on the measuring tool without being asked, then the worn-smooth spot where his thumb had lived for years, and the tool came out the way an old friend comes out of a quiet room.
Now this,
spans.speaker: Patch

spans.text: he said,
is a proper builder's problem.
spans.speaker: Patch

spans.text: He looked at the ramps stacked into the canyon like giant stairs. He looked at the rail lines curling between cactus towers, catching the morning light along their tops and running it forward in thin shining ribbons that pinged faintly in the heat. He looked at the moving platform swinging on a slow patient hinge. He looked at a red button on a square block at the edge of a track, trembling under a hand-painted sign that read PRESS ME GENTLY, the paint touched up at least four times, the most recent touch only a few days old.
I can fix that,
spans.speaker: Patch

spans.text: Patch said.

He said it the way he had said it his whole life. The way a builder says it when he has built more brackets than he has eaten meals. He did not hear the way the canyon took the sentence and gave nothing back. The canyon did not echo. It absorbed. His words went out across the warm sandstone, dropped into the rock, and stopped existing.

An old desert mechanic in a gear-marked hat climbed onto a ledge and waved both arms. His goggles glowed blue. His moustache was white as an old letter read too many times, and it bounced when he shouted.
Howdy, builders. I am Dusty Gear, and if you could avoid standing on the boulder line, that would make this introduction friendlier for everybody.
The crew looked down at their boots. Nobody was standing on a boulder line, mostly because nobody knew what one was yet.

Dusty Gear winced. It was a polite wince, the wince of a man who had heard many opening sentences and had come to know a certain optimistic flavor that the canyon, by midmorning, would correct out of them.
That,
spans.speaker: Dusty Gear

spans.text: he said,
is what the last three route mechanics said.
spans.speaker: Dusty Gear

spans.text: The crew went still.
Last three,
spans.speaker: Pip

spans.text: Pip Pop repeated.
Last three.
spans.speaker: Pip

spans.text: That seems like a lot of mechanics,
spans.speaker: Brick

spans.text: Brick Bloom said carefully.
Sand Canyon is a generous canyon,
spans.speaker: Dusty Gear

spans.text: Dusty Gear said.
It gives you all the chances you can stand. Sometimes a few more than that, to be polite.
spans.speaker: Dusty Gear

spans.text: He climbed down. Sandstone dust fell off his boots in tidy little squares, the way canyon sandstone did and other sandstone did not, and the squares held their shape on the floor a beat longer than dust had any business holding a shape, then slumped, slow, the way a small carefully made pile slumps when no one is looking. He did it without thinking. The canyon did it along with him.
Stand still a moment. I will do the welcome the canyon prefers, and then we will get into the trouble.
spans.speaker: Dusty Gear

spans.text: Patch tried to stand still. He got most of the way there.

His body stood. His hand crouched it at the nearest rail. The rail was warm under his palm, not hot, warm the way a pan is warm an hour after use. He had built rails in Green Hills out of slick green polymer that matched the temperature of the air, which was no temperature at all. This rail had been baked by a high sun for a long time and it remembered the sun in its metal. He set the tool to it. Six squares to the inside flange. Standard gauge, but wider than he had expected. He noted that, and stored the noting in a place inside him that had no name yet, only entries.
A heavy hand came down on his shoulder.
Patch,
spans.speaker: Moss

spans.text: Moss Guard said.
Sorry.
Stand still.
Sorry.

Moss did not move his hand. He let it rest. It was the weight of a guardian's hand, not a controlling weight but a present one, a hand the size of a sandstone block that said I am here, and you are also here, and the rest of you can stop now. Patch let the tool hang loose at his side. He felt the canyon hum up through Moss's hand into his shoulder, his spine, the soles of his boots.
It was not a hum you could complain about. It was the kind you noticed once and then knew had been there the whole time.
Click. Wait. Slide. Click.

The click sat in his ankles. The wait sat behind his knees. The slide ran the backs of his thighs. The second click landed in the small of his back. Four parts of a beat, divvied across four parts of him. He had stood on a great many floors. None of them had divided itself across his body this way. The Green Hills floor had been the same beat as the air, which was no beat. This floor had a four-part beat, and his body had taken up the four parts without asking his permission.

He had not asked his measuring tool to listen for that. The tool was not built to. It read distances, and distances were honest, and the canyon's wait was not a distance, so the tool sat in his hand and reported, politely, that everything was fine.
He noticed the small mismatch.
He stored it.
Welcome,
spans.speaker: Dusty Gear

spans.text: Dusty Gear said,

to Sand Canyon. We have ramps. We have rails. We have switches. We have moving platforms, sliding stones, rolling crates, and at least one boulder line we are not currently friends with. You will hear the canyon humming. That hum is the timing. You ignore the hum and the canyon ignores you back, often loudly.
spans.speaker: Dusty Gear

spans.text: He pointed up at the trembling red button.
That is Sandy Switch. He is shy. He likes to be pressed gently and not yelled at, and he is the only gate switch we have, so we are doing our best to keep his mood up.
Sandy Switch trembled. From a distance the trembling looked like an apology in advance for whatever the canyon was about to do.
Welcome, friends,
spans.speaker: Sandy

spans.text: Sandy whispered.
Hello, Sandy,
spans.speaker: Brick

spans.text: Brick said warmly, and Sandy trembled in a more hopeful direction.
The route crate,
spans.speaker: Dusty Gear

spans.text: Dusty Gear went on,

is supposed to roll down the main rail, take the moving platform at the right beat, hit Sandy from a respectful angle, and open the canyon gate. It has not been doing that. It has been taking the side rail, missing Sandy entirely, and waking the boulder line.
spans.speaker: Dusty Gear

spans.text: What is the boulder line,
spans.speaker: Captain

spans.text: Captain Cubemelon asked.

He had lifted the Gravity Wrench when the rumble came, and he was holding it now by its middle, not its handle. The middle was a less ready grip. It did not whisper ask me. It let him carry the wrench the way a person carries a walking stick, a thing to lean on rather than a thing to swing. He had decided, on the portal hop over, that this would be Patch's build, and that decision was turning out to be a long series of small refusals, each of which cost him something. Do not lift the wrench. Do not measure. Do not correct. He held the middle. His thumb found a ridge it had never bothered to find before.
A line of boulders that used to live high on the cliff,
spans.speaker: Dusty Gear

spans.text: Dusty Gear said.

Now they live in a holding loop up there, and they only come down if something hits the wrong switch hard. We would prefer they keep living in the loop. They are excellent boulders. They just need to stay where they are.
spans.speaker: Dusty Gear

spans.text: Excellent how,
spans.speaker: Ember

spans.text: Ember asked.
Excellent in the sense of large, round, and consistent. The canyon does not breed mediocre boulders. This is a high-standards canyon.
spans.speaker: Dusty Gear

spans.text: Patch tilted his head back. The cliff ran for what looked like a quarter mile, warm orange sandstone streaked with bands of darker rust, and near the top, at the edge of his sight, he found them: a line of round shadows tucked into a long curving channel, sitting where they had been told to sit, looking from down here like an old necklace someone had hung on a peg and forgotten.
He counted seven.
Then he stopped, because seven might be only the ones he could see. The thought arrived too large to do anything with yet. He set it down beside the measuring tool.
The boulder line only came down if something hit the wrong switch hard,
spans.speaker: Dusty Gear

spans.text: Dusty Gear said, following his eyes.
It had come down once already, and it was still counting.
spans.speaker: Dusty Gear

spans.text: Patch heard that as the kind of sentence a builder files and does not yet feel. He filed it.
He stared at the rail line. He stared at the moving platform, the gauge, the angle of the side rail's diverging switch.
I can fix this,

he said again. Quieter this time, and more careful, with the weight of a builder who had just heard, for the first time, the canyon's low patient click-wait-slide-click coming from somewhere under the dust.
That is the canyon,
spans.speaker: Dusty Gear

spans.text: Dusty Gear said.
That is the timing. You will get used to it.
spans.speaker: Dusty Gear

spans.text: I am already getting used to it,
spans.speaker: Patch

spans.text: Patch said.
He did not yet know how much of a lie that was.

The thing was, he had felt this once before, and the feeling had a face he did not know he was making. It had happened in Green Hills, on a bright clean tutorial morning. In Green Hills he had built a ramp at exactly the angle the math required, and it had launched Pip Pop two squares too far, and the number had been right and the throw had been wrong, and he had never once thought the number could be the problem. He had measured the ramp again afterward. The ramp had been correct. The throw had still been wrong. He had filed the contradiction in the nameless inner place and had been carrying it, quietly, ever since, the way you carry a small stone in a boot you keep meaning to empty.
He looked at the canyon. He looked at the cliff. The contradiction stirred in the boot.

The canyon answered him the way it answered everyone. It clicked. It waited. It slid. It clicked. And up in the boulder line, that single rounded shadow shifted its quarter inch again and settled, patient, like a thing that had all morning and most of the afternoon to wait him out.

Captain saw the shift. He did not mention it. He was watching Patch's face, where the brow over the left goggle had drawn down a quarter inch and the lips had pressed to a thin line at one corner, the exact look Patch had made in Green Hills the day the correct ramp threw Pip wrong. Captain had filed that look under things to never point out. He had spent the week before Sand Canyon practicing reading Patch without saying a word, because today the reading would be the only way he could lead without leading.
That had been a small wrong angle.
Looking at Patch's face now, Captain suspected this one was a great deal bigger.

He kept the suspicion to himself. He kept his hand on the middle of the wrench. The wanting to lift it arrived, the way it would keep arriving for as long as he was a leader, and he let it pass through his hands like wind through a window and did not let it reach his fingers.
Ember drifted up beside him, looking at the canyon and not at him, which was her way of asking a question without asking it.
That was the fastest crate I have ever seen,
spans.speaker: Ember

spans.text: she said.
Yes.
spans.speaker: Captain

spans.text: It went past me before I could decide to chase it.
spans.speaker: Ember

spans.text: Yes.
spans.speaker: Captain

spans.text: I do not think I can outrun this canyon.
spans.speaker: Ember

spans.text: No,
spans.speaker: Captain

spans.text: Captain said.

She nodded once, small, and turned and walked slow toward the arch the crate had vanished behind. Walking slow in Sand Canyon was a different thing than walking slow in Green Hills. The slabs shifted under her boots, small shifts, on the canyon's beat, when she paid attention. Walking on the canyon was a beat too. She filed that, and did not test it, and felt very mature about not testing it.

Patch barely heard any of it. He was looking up at the boulders, and down at the diverging switch, and the warm tape on his tool ran warmer than it ever had, and the small stone shifted in the boot, and he thought, with the whole confidence of a builder who had built more brackets than he had eaten meals: I can fix that.
He did not yet know how much of a lie that was, either.
